summary:
Orbit lab is an interactive educational space mission simulator website that allows students to design, build, launch, and operate their own satellite. It addresses the challenge of teaching complex space mission design by turning engineering concepts into practical, engaging experiments.
The project features 12 unique missions and a catalog of 18 real-world space technologies across six categories: scientific instruments, solar panels, batteries, communication systems, orbits, and launch vehicles. Students must balance budgets, spacecraft mass, power consumption, data storage, communication windows, and scientific objectives. They also face unexpected mission hazards and make decisions that affect mission outcomes.
The simulator supports five languages, local teamwork for up to four players, mission reports, and persistent progress tracking. Its scientific references distinguish published specifications from simulation estimates.
Orbit lab is important because it makes space engineering more accessible, encourages systems thinking and problem solving, and helps students understand how real engineering trade-offs shape successful space missions.
details:
Orbit lab is an interactive educational space mission simulator website designed to help students understand how real satellite missions are planned, assembled, launched, and operated. Instead of learning about spacecraft engineering through theory alone, students can experiment with engineering decisions and observe how each choice affects the mission.

What does the project do and how does it work?

The simulator takes students through the complete lifecycle of an educational Earth observation mission. It offers 12 different missions, including monitoring agricultural health, coastal erosion, wildfires, floods, polar ice, nighttime lights, and atmospheric conditions. Each mission has its own scientific objectives, requirements, challenges, and engineering constraints.

Students enter a spacecraft workshop where they select components from six main categories: scientific instruments, solar panels, batteries, communication systems, orbital configurations, and launch vehicles. The project includes 18 catalog entries based on real space products and systems, supported by manufacturer information and scientific references. Every choice has consequences. A more capable instrument may produce more useful scientific data but also increase power consumption and storage requirements. A faster communication system may improve data delivery but require additional electrical power. Students must balance spacecraft mass, mission budget, battery capacity, energy generation, data storage, communication opportunities, and scientific objectives.

After assembling their spacecraft, students proceed through a launch sequence and enter mission control. They can operate the satellite manually or use an autopilot system, control the scientific instrument, manage communication, monitor resources, and respond to unexpected hazards. The simulation includes 24 different emergency events, each presenting decisions that can change mission performance.

At the end, students receive a mission report explaining their results, resource usage, decisions, and areas for improvement.

What benefits does it have?

Orbit lab makes complex aerospace engineering concepts easier to understand through experimentation. Students learn that successful space missions require more than choosing powerful equipment: every subsystem must work together within strict engineering limits. The project develops critical thinking, problem solving skills, scientific reasoning, resource management, and decision-making skills. It also encourages students to learn from mistakes by allowing them to redesign their spacecraft and try different engineering approaches.

The simulator supports five languages: Arabic, English, French, German, and Spanish. It also includes a collaborative mode for up to four players on the same device, allowing students to share responsibilities as mission commander, systems engineer, science specialist, and power and communications officer.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using:

  • HTML for the application structure and interface.
  • CSS for visual design, responsive layouts, animations, and interface styling.
  • JavaScript for application logic, spacecraft configuration, simulation calculations, mission management, and interactions.
  • SVG illustrations for spacecraft components, orbital diagrams, and launch vehicle visuals.
  • Web Audio API for generated sound effects and alerts.
  • Browser Local Storage for saving mission progress, campaign data, selected designs, upgrades, and settings.

What makes the project creative?

Its main creative idea is combining a spacecraft building experience with a mission management simulation. Students do not simply answer questions or select predefined solutions; they build a spacecraft configuration, face engineering trade-offs, operate their mission, and learn from the consequences.

The workshop visually reflects component selections, while the launch sequence and cockpit-inspired Mission Control interface help create an engaging experience. Randomized hazards introduce uncertainty and require students to make meaningful decisions under time pressure.

Another important feature is the separation between published technical specifications and educational simulation estimates. Real product information is connected to its sources, while game credits are clearly distinguished from actual commercial prices.

What factors did we consider?

During development, we focused on scientific accuracy, educational value, usability, accessibility, performance, and maintainability. We considered the relationships between mass, power, storage, communications, orbital conditions, and mission objectives. We also considered multilingual support, preservation of player progress, responsive design, and the importance of explaining complex engineering concepts clearly.

The simulation is intentionally educational rather than a professional spacecraft engineering tool. Where exact public specifications are unavailable, assumptions and limitations are documented rather than presented as scientific facts.

Intended impact

Our goal is to make space engineering more accessible and engaging, especially for students who may never have the opportunity to experiment with an entire space mission. Orbit lab aims to transform students from passive learners into mission designers who think like engineers, test their ideas, manage constraints, collaborate, and understand how scientific knowledge becomes a real-world space mission.
